# Streaming, Worked Out

> An interactive, single-page explainer for streaming over HTTP: why a response is allowed to stay
> open (chunked transfer coding), what Server-Sent Events actually specifies, how `EventSource`
> reconnection and `Last-Event-ID` work, how an AI model's tokens arrive as an SSE stream, and how to
> consume one in TypeScript without losing a character to a chunk boundary. The SSE parser, the
> WHATWG dispatch rules, the UTF-8 decoder behaviour and the two resumption designs are verified
> against real running code by `test-model.ts`. Author: Paweł Pasek.

Key points made on this page:

- **Three facts about any stream** — (1) the pieces are not yours to choose: one `write()` on the
  server is not one `read()` on the client, so code that assumes "one write, one message" is correct
  on localhost and wrong in production; (2) therefore a stream needs a framing rule, because "no more
  bytes yet" and "no more bytes ever" look identical — SSE's is a blank line, a model turn's is
  `content_block_stop`; (3) a stream can stop mid-flight, and only the receiver knows what arrived,
  which is why resumption is a header the client sends.
- **Chunked transfer coding** — RFC 9112: "Chunked enables content streams of unknown size to be
  transferred as a sequence of length-delimited buffers." A streaming endpoint simply never sends the
  terminating zero-length chunk. Call `res.flushHeaders()` or the headers wait for your first event.
- **The SSE wire format** — lines of `field: value`; a blank line dispatches. `data:` (multiple lines
  join with newlines), `event:` (type for `addEventListener`, default `"message"`), `id:` (resumption
  checkpoint), `retry:` (reconnection time in ms), and a leading `:` marks a comment used as a
  keep-alive. The field name is everything before the *first* colon, so JSON payloads are safe. The
  spec rule that causes the most bugs: "the last still has to end with a blank line, the end of the
  stream is not enough to trigger the dispatch of the last event."
- **EventSource** — gives you parsing, dispatch by type and automatic reconnection announcing
  `Last-Event-ID`. It cannot set request headers (including `Authorization`), cannot POST or send a
  body, and never stops retrying. Real code usually moves to `fetch` + `ReadableStream` for the first
  of those reasons. Resumption is a two-sided contract: the browser sends the header, but a server
  that ignores it replays duplicates forever. Replaying a whole bounded buffer instead is a valid
  design, but only paired with a client that de-duplicates by id.
- **AI model streaming** — the same mechanism with a documented schema: `message_start` → per-block
  `content_block_start`/`content_block_delta`/`content_block_stop` → `message_delta` →
  `message_stop`, with `ping` as a typed keep-alive. Tool-call arguments arrive as `input_json_delta`
  fragments (`partial_json`) that are only guaranteed parseable once the block closes — fact 2 one
  level up the stack.
- **Consuming in TypeScript** — `fetch` + `res.body.getReader()` + a `TextDecoder`. Two buffers are
  in play: the parser holds a partial *line*, the decoder holds partial *bytes*. Decode with
  `{ stream: true }`, or a multi-byte character split across chunks becomes `U+FFFD` permanently and
  silently. Cancel with `AbortController` and treat `AbortError` as a normal exit.
- **SSE vs WebSocket vs long-polling** — SSE is one-directional ordinary HTTP, so proxies, auth and
  observability already work; WebSocket is a protocol upgrade worth taking when upward traffic is
  *continuous*, not merely present, and you inherit its heartbeats and resumption yourself. A stream
  down plus ordinary POSTs up is a perfectly good bidirectional system. The one genuine SSE limit is
  browser connection count: six per browser on HTTP/1.1, negotiated (default 100) on HTTP/2.
- **What goes wrong** — a buffering proxy (nginx `proxy_buffering off`, or send
  `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), compression that doesn't flush, load-balancer idle timeouts, no cleanup
  on disconnect (a leaked listener per drop), assuming one write is one message, and ignoring
  backpressure when `res.write()` returns false. Diagnostic: `curl -N` direct versus through the
  proxy; if only the direct one streams, nothing in your application code is wrong.

## Page

- [Streaming, Worked Out](https://pasekpasek.github.io/streaming-worked-out/): the full explainer.

## Source material

- [RFC 9112 §7.1 — HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer coding](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-7.1)
- [WHATWG HTML — Server-Sent Events](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html): the wire format, the parsing algorithm, and the `Last-Event-ID` header.
- [WHATWG Encoding — TextDecoder.decode()](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-textdecoder-decode): the `stream` option and fragmented input.
- [MDN — Using server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events): the six-connection HTTP/1.1 limit.
- [Anthropic Messages API — streaming](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming): the "Streaming request with tool use" response quoted verbatim as this page's §06 fixture.
- [4th-devs](https://github.com/i-am-alice/4th-devs), `05_01_agent_graph/src/{server.ts,events.ts}`: the SSE handler and in-process event bus this page quotes.

## Caveat

Four of the page's models are checked by `test-model.ts` (15 checks): the SSE parser against a real
`node:http` server with an event split across two TCP-level writes, the WHATWG dispatch rules, the
UTF-8 chunk-boundary behaviour against the real `TextDecoder`, and the two resumption designs. The
RFC, spec and MDN statements are quoted from those documents rather than reproduced. The §06
streaming fixture is quoted from Anthropic's own published documentation, not captured from a live
API call.
